title: The Birth, Life and Death of Stars
seo_title: Grade 9 Natural Sciences: The Birth, Life and Death of Stars Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_code: Grade 9 Natural Sciences: Birth, life and death of stars
standard_text: Stars form from clouds of gas and dust (nebulae); they shine by nuclear fusion; the life cycle of a star depends on its mass (red giant and white dwarf, or supergiant, supernova and neutron star or black hole). The Sun is a medium-sized star. (summary of CAPS Natural Sciences, Grade 9, Planet Earth and Beyond: Birth, life and death of stars)
meta_desc: Free Grade 9 Natural Sciences worksheets (CAPS): nebulae, nuclear fusion, main-sequence stars, red giants, white dwarfs, supernovae and black holes. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: A star's mass decides how it ends.
body_html:
How to think about it

Stars form when gravity pulls together a cloud of gas and dust called a nebula. When the centre becomes hot enough, hydrogen nuclei fuse to make helium, releasing energy: the star shines. Most of a star's life is spent as a main-sequence star, like the Sun.

A star like the Sun swells into a red giant and ends as a white dwarf. A very massive star becomes a red supergiant, explodes as a supernova and leaves a neutron star or a black hole. Supernovae spread heavy elements that form new stars and planets.

Example

What process makes stars shine?

Hydrogen to helium

Answer: nuclear fusion

Example

How will the Sun end its life?

It is a medium-sized star.

Answer: as a white dwarf

Common mistakes

  • Thinking stars burn like fires.
  • Thinking all stars become black holes.
  • Thinking the Sun is a very large star.

items.q: Evidence: A faint microwave glow comes evenly from every direction in the sky. What does it support?
c: The early universe was hot, dense and very uniform, then cooled as it expanded.
This is leftover radiation from the hot early universe (the CMB).
We see them as they were billions of years ago, when the universe was younger.
items.e: Three main lines of evidence: redshift, the CMB and light-element abundances.

items.q: Which evidence supports this idea: “Space itself is stretching everywhere (Hubble's law).”
c: Almost every distant galaxy's light is redshifted.
About 75% of normal matter is hydrogen and about 25% is helium.
The farther a galaxy is, the faster it moves away.
Very distant galaxies look younger and less developed.
items.e: Match the evidence to the idea.
